title: Travis Kalanick’s Atoms might be getting into the robotaxi business
content:
Earlier this summer, Travis Kalanick’s Atoms announced a $1.7 billion funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz. But even after raising that mega round, the Uber founder remained a bit cagey about what he was actually aiming to do.
Now a story in the Financial Times offers more details about Atoms’ goals. The startup is reportedly preparing for a hiring spree, as well as acquisitions, that could make it a major player in the autonomous vehicle industry.
In fact, the FT said Atoms has talked to Uber about how the ride-hailing company could use the startup’s robotaxi technology. (Uber has already partnered with a long list of autonomous vehicle companies.) The report also noted that Uber has invested $100 million in Atoms — a figure previously confirmed by TechCrunch.
While sources emphasized that robotaxis don’t represent the entirety of Atoms’ plans, this direction seems consistent with Kalanick’s description of the round as “unfinished business.”
It also fits with Atoms’ acquisition of Pronto, an autonomous mining startup led by Uber’s former self-driving chief Anthony Levandowski. (Levandowski was convicted of stealing trade secrets and sentenced to 18 months in prison, but was then pardoned by President Donald Trump.)

report.summary: Travis Kalanick's startup Atoms is reportedly expanding into robotaxis, with Uber talks and acquisition plans reported.
report.background: Atoms, founded by Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, raised a $1.7 billion round earlier this summer led by Andreessen Horowitz, but kept its exact strategy vague. New reports from the Financial Times suggest Atoms is preparing to become a major autonomous vehicle player through hiring and acquisitions. The company has reportedly held discussions with Uber about integrating its robotaxi technology, and Uber has already invested $100 million in Atoms. Atoms previously acquired Pronto, an autonomous mining startup led by Anthony Levandowski, Uber's former self-driving chief who was convicted of trade secret theft and later pardoned. Kalanick has described his latest venture as “unfinished business,” hinting at a return to the ride-hailing and mobility space he helped pioneer, though sources indicate robotaxis are not the entirety of Atoms' plans.
key_points: Atoms is reportedly planning a major push into autonomous vehicles, including robotaxis, according to a Financial Times report. The startup is said to be preparing a hiring spree and potential acquisitions to scale up its AV capabilities quickly.

Atoms has discussed with Uber how its robotaxi technology could be used by the ride-hailing giant. Uber has already invested $100 million in Atoms, confirming a financial and strategic tie between the two companies, even as Uber partners with many AV firms.

Kalanick's earlier description of the $1.7 billion funding round as 'unfinished business' now appears more clear: returning to the mobility sector and competing in autonomous ride-hailing, an area Uber itself has long pursued through partnerships.

Atoms' acquisition of Pronto, led by formerly convicted Anthony Levandowski, signals a focus on autonomous systems. Levandowski's background in self-driving tech, despite legal controversies, could bring deep expertise to Atoms' robotaxi efforts.

Sources caution that robotaxis are only part of Atoms' broader plans. The company may be building a diversified autonomous vehicle portfolio, though robotaxi development appears to be a central near-term focus, potentially putting it in direct competition with Waymo, Tesla, and others.
report.impact: If Atoms enters the robotaxi market, it could intensify competition in an already crowded field, pushing down prices and accelerating deployment of autonomous ride-hailing. For developers and AV engineers, this could mean more job opportunities and a stronger talent war, especially given Atoms' reported hiring spree. For regular users, more players may lead to faster rollout in more cities and more choices, but also raises safety and regulatory questions, especially because of Levandowski's history. Uber's investment suggests it sees Atoms as a complement rather than a competitor, but Kalanick's return to mobility could reshape industry alliances and force incumbents to innovate faster.
report.tools: For those tracking robotaxi and AV developments, watch open-source tools like Autoware and Apollo (Baidu's open-source self-driving platform), as well as datasets like nuScenes and Lyft Level 5. Companies to monitor include Waymo, Cruise, Zoox, and Aurora. Given Atoms' reported plans, official announcements, job postings, and regulatory filings will be useful to follow closely.
